content: The Department of Paediatrics and Child Health at Aga Khan University in Karachi, Pakistan, is a key institution contributing to advancements in child health. Jemima Dennis-Antwi, an international consultant in midwifery based in West Legon, Accra, Ghana, provides expertise in maternal and newborn care. Luz Maria de-Regil, Vice President of Global Technical Services and Chief Technical Advisor at the Micronutrient Initiative in Ottawa, Canada, focuses on global nutrition interventions, including calcium supplementation during pregnancy in lowand middle-income countries. Christine East, a Professor of Midwifery at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, specializes in maternity services and midwifery education. Lynn Freedman, Director of the Averting Maternal Death and Disability Program at Columbia University in New York, USA, is a leading expert in maternal health. Pisake Lumbiganon, a Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Khon Kaen University in Thailand, is the convenor of Cochrane Thailand and contributes to evidence-based obstetric care. Anita Maepioh, a nurse educator at the National Referral Hospital in Honiara, Solomon Islands, focuses on obstetrics and gynaecology training. James Neilson, Vice-Chair of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and a member of the Department of Women’s and Children’s Health at the University of Liverpool, UK, contributes to maternal and child health research. Hiromi Obara, a Health Policy Advisor with the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) in Vientiane, Lao PDR, provides expertise in reproductive health policy. Zahida Qureshi, Chair of the GDG and Associate Professor at the University of Nairobi in Kenya, specializes in obstetrics and gynaecology. Kathleen Rasmussen, a Professor of Maternal and Child Nutrition at Cornell University in New York, USA, focuses on nutritional sciences. Niveen Abu Rmeileh, Director of the Institute of Community and Public Health at Birzeit University in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, contributes to public health initiatives. Eleni Tsigas, CEO of the Preeclampsia Foundation in the USA, represents patient experiences related to hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. A.A. Visser, Chair of the FIGO Committee on Safe Motherhood and Newborn Health at the University Medical Center Utrecht in the Netherlands, is an expert in obstetrics. Charlotte Warren, Director of the Ending Eclampsia Project at the Population Council in Washington, DC, USA, focuses on maternal and newborn health. The systematic review team includes Anna Cuthbert, Leanne Jones, Frances Kellie, and Myfanwy Williams, all research associates or managing editors at the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group Editorial Office at the University of Liverpool, UK. WHO country and regional officers, such as Nino Berdzuli (Europe), Bremen De Mucio (Americas), Chandani Anoma Jayathilaka (South-East Asia), Ramez Khairi Mahaini (Eastern Mediterranean), Léopold Ouedraogo (Africa), and Howard Sobel (Western Pacific), contribute to sexual, reproductive, maternal, and child health initiatives. The WHO steering group, led by A. Metin Gülmezoglu, Ana Pilar Betrán, Mercedes Bonet, Olufemi T. Oladapo, David Stenson, Özge Tunçalp, and Joshua P. Vogel, focuses on maternal and perinatal health and preventing unsafe abortion. The Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health includes Maurice Bucagu, Fran McConville, and Anayda Portela, who work on policy, planning, and research development. External reviewers such as José Guilherme Cecatti (Brazil), Sylvia Deganus (Ghana), Nguyen Xuan Hoi (Vietnam), Jack Moodley (South Africa), Jane Sandall (UK), M. Jeeva Sankar (India), Hayfaa Wahabi (Saudi Arabia), and Ola Shaker Hussien Salama (Egypt) provide expertise in obstetrics, gynaecology, midwifery, and evidence-based healthcare. The WHO recommendations address the management of severe pre-eclampsia before term, comparing interventionist care (immediate delivery) with expectant management (monitoring and delayed delivery). Maternal outcomes include risks of eclampsia, recurrent seizures, ICU admission, severe morbidity, and death. Fetal outcomes include Apgar scores, NICU admissions, and perinatal death. Evidence from six trials involving 748 women suggests varying effects, with some studies indicating potential harm to neonates in the interventionist group, such as intraventricular hemorrhage and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. The GDG emphasizes the importance of involving women in decision-making, valuing perinatal outcomes, and addressing health inequities, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Implementation challenges include resource availability, healthcare provider training, and community engagement. Effective communication between women and healthcare providers is critical for successful implementation of interventions.
